usage: 값 takes 이 because it ends in a consonant
비싸다 is the standard opposite of 싸다
to knock the price down, to haggle
깎다 literally 'to shave off' — the verb for bargaining
치르다 is more formal/literary than 내다
examples: 이 신발 값이 싸요.
These shoes are cheap.
noun + 값이 + adjective is the basic frame
물건은 좋은데 값이 너무 비싸요.
The item is good, but the price is too high.
-는데 sets up a contrast before the complaint
시장에서는 값을 좀 깎을 수 있어요.
At a traditional market you can haggle the price down a bit.
-을 수 있다 = to be able to; 시장 implies bargaining is okay
nuance: 값 is the pure native-Korean word for the price or worth of a thing, and it feels more everyday and spoken than the Sino-Korean 가격 (價格), which sounds printed and store-like (a tag reads 가격, but you say 값이 싸다). The dividing line: 값 leans casual and is the half that lives inside set verb phrases, while 가격 is neutral-formal and abstract. 값 is also more than money — 값어치 means 'worth/value', so it carries a nuance of deserved cost. It bonds with 싸다/비싸다 for cheap/expensive and with 깎다 (to shave off) for haggling, plus the fixed 값을 치르다 (to pay the price, even figuratively). English pitfall: do not say 값 비싸요 — the subject particle is obligatory, so it must be 값이 비싸요. And never use 비싸다 for an action's cost; 비싸다 only describes the price of an object, not an activity.

Translating 'the trip's price' as 여행 값 — for the cost of an activity use 비용 (비용이 들다); 값 is for a concrete item.

usage: 잔돈 + 이 없다 = to not have
잔돈 + 을, the thing handed over
to break (a bill) into small change
으로 marks the result you change something into
모자라다 = to fall short, run low
examples: 죄송한데 잔돈이 없어요.
Sorry, but I don't have any small change.
죄송한데 softens a refusal — very common at a register
혹시 잔돈 좀 주실 수 있어요?
Could you possibly give me some change?
혹시 + 좀 makes the request gentle and polite
오천 원을 천 원짜리 잔돈으로 바꿨어요.
I broke a 5,000 won bill into 1,000 won change.
X을 Y으로 바꾸다 = change X into Y; past tense 바꿨어요
nuance: 잔돈 is built from 잔- (the native root in 잘다, 'fine/small') plus 돈 (money), so it literally means 'small money' — the coins and low bills you carry. Its near-synonym is 거스름돈, and the dividing line is direction: 거스름돈 is specifically the change handed back to you after you overpay, while 잔돈 is any small money you already hold (and is often used for 거스름돈 too in casual speech). Note 잔돈 is one solid word, never 잔 돈. It collocates with 없다 (not have), 모자라다 (run short), and 바꾸다 (to break a bill). A cashier asking 잔돈 있으세요? means 'Do you have the exact small change?' so they can give round bills back. English pitfall: don't think of it as 'spare change' you give away to charity — that idea is 잔돈/푼돈 only loosely; 잔돈 is neutral pocket change, not a moral 'leftover'.

usage: 세다 = to count, used for countable notes
examples: 만 원짜리 지폐 있어요?
Do you have a 10,000 won bill?
짜리 attaches to the amount to name the denomination
잔돈이 없어서 지폐로 낼게요.
I have no coins, so I'll pay with a bill.
-아서/어서 gives the reason; -ㄹ게요 states your intention
은행에서 새 지폐로 바꿔 달라고 했어요.
I asked the bank to exchange it for crisp new bills.
-아 달라고 하다 = to ask someone to do something for you
nuance: 지폐 is Sino-Korean 紙幣, literally 'paper (紙) + currency (幣)', so it precisely names paper money as a physical form, in contrast to 동전 (銅錢, copper-coin) for coins. Its near-synonym 돈 is the general word for money, while 지폐 zooms in on the bills themselves; another relative is 현금 (cash, as opposed to card), which can be bills or coins. So the line is: 지폐 = paper notes specifically, 현금 = cash in any form, 돈 = money in the abstract. It is calm and neutral, equally fine in speech and writing, and pairs with 세다 (count), 바꾸다 (exchange), and the denomination pattern 만 원짜리. English pitfall: never stretch 지폐 to cover coins — coins are strictly 동전. Also, in casual speech Koreans usually just say the amount + 짜리 (만 원짜리), reserving 지폐 for when paper money is being contrasted with coins or cards.

Saying just 만 원 지폐 — to name a denomination you need 짜리: 만 원짜리 지폐.
Equating 지폐 with 현금 — 현금 (cash) can include coins, so they are not interchangeable when the form matters.

usage: 맞다 = to be right/correct, used for figures
확인하다, the standard verb at a counter
money amounts are 크다/작다, not 많다/적다
examples: 금액이 맞아요?
Is the amount correct?
a natural check when the cashier states a price
결제하기 전에 총 금액을 확인했어요.
I checked the total amount before paying.
-기 전에 = before doing; 총 금액 = grand total
이체할 금액을 잘못 입력했어요.
I entered the wrong amount for the transfer.
이체 = bank transfer; 입력하다 = to type/input
nuance: 금액 is Sino-Korean 金額, literally 'money (金) + amount (額)', so it means a specific stated sum written on a bill, receipt, or screen. Its near-synonym is 액수, which also means 'a sum/figure'; the dividing line is feel — 금액 is the everyday counter-and-banking word (you see 총 금액 at checkout), while 액수 sounds slightly more abstract or written ('the figure involved'). Against plain 돈, 금액 is the precise quantity, not money in general. Crucially, a 금액 is described as 크다/작다 (big/small), not 많다/적다, because it is a single value rather than a countable heap. It collocates with 확인하다 (verify), 맞다 (be correct), 입력하다 (input), and 총. English pitfall: do not use 금액 to mean 'money' broadly — '돈이 없어요' (I have no money), never '금액이 없어요'. And ask 금액이 얼마예요?, keeping the obligatory 이.

Dropping the particle in 금액 얼마예요 — say 금액이 얼마예요?.

usage: 합계 + 가, asking the bottom-line figure
to add up / work out the total
내다 here = to produce a result
examples: 전부 합계가 얼마예요?
What's the grand total for everything?
전부 = all of it, reinforcing the sum
영수증에 합계가 찍혀 있어요.
The total is printed on the receipt.
찍히다 = to be stamped/printed (passive)
엑셀에서 이 칸들의 합계를 냈어요.
I worked out the sum of these cells in Excel.
합계를 내다 = to compute a total
nuance: 합계 is Sino-Korean 合計, literally 'combine (合) + count/reckon (計)', so it is the figure you get after adding everything together — the bottom line. Its near-synonyms are 총액 (總額, 'total sum') and the phrasal 총 금액; all three appear at checkout. The dividing line is tone: 합계 emphasizes the act of summing items (it pairs with 내다, 'to total up') and reads like a printed label on receipts and spreadsheets, whereas 총액/총 금액 simply name the resulting grand figure. So you write 합계 in a column header but more often say 총 얼마예요? aloud. It collocates with 내다 (to compute), 나오다 (to come out), and 금액. English pitfall: do not confuse the look-alike pair — 합계 (total) versus 할인 (割引, discount); they share 합/할 onset but are opposites. Also keep it as one word, 합계, never 합 계.

examples: 이 상품은 인기가 많아요.
This product is very popular.
인기가 많다 is the set phrase for 'popular'
온라인몰에 상품이 정말 다양해요.
The online mall has a really wide range of products.
다양해요 describes selection, not quantity
오늘 들어온 신상품을 진열했어요.
I put out the new products that came in today.
신상품 = new product; 진열하다 = to display
nuance: 상품 is Sino-Korean 商品, literally 'commerce (商) + article (品)', so it is the store-and-marketing word for goods that are for sale — what you see on price tags, signs, and shopping sites (신상품 'new product', 인기 상품, 할인 상품). Its near-synonym is the native 물건, and the dividing line is for-sale-ness and register: 상품 implies merchandise being sold and sounds slightly formal/commercial, while 물건 is the casual catch-all for any 'thing' or your personal belongings. So a shop stocks 상품 but you grab your own 물건 before leaving. It collocates with 고르다 (choose), 다양하다 (be varied), and the modifiers 인기/할인/신. English pitfall: do not call your own possessions 상품 — 'my stuff' is 내 물건, never 내 상품. Also keep 상품 (product) distinct from the look-alike 상품권 (gift voucher).

english: regular customer; a place one frequents
usage: a shop one goes to regularly
단골 + 이 되다 = to turn into
단골 + 손님, the full unambiguous form
examples: 여기는 제 단골 가게예요.
This is my go-to shop.
제 = my (humble); 가게 = small store
저는 이 카페 단골이라서 사장님이 알아봐요.
I'm a regular at this cafe, so the owner recognizes me.
-라서 = because; 알아보다 = to recognize
단골이 되면 가끔 서비스를 주세요.
Once you become a regular, they sometimes give you free extras.
-면 = when/if; 서비스 here means a free add-on
nuance: 단골 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) that names the loyal, repeating relationship between a customer and a shop — and remarkably it works both directions: it can mean the regular customer (단골손님) or the favorite place itself (단골 가게). Its near-synonym is the Sino-Korean 고객 (顧客, 'client/customer'), but the dividing line is warmth and loyalty: 고객 is any neutral customer (a 'valued customer' in business-speak), whereas 단골 carries the cozy nuance of someone who keeps coming back and gets remembered. Becoming a 단골 in Korea often earns friendlier service, a 서비스 (free side or extra), or a small discount. It collocates with 되다 (become), 가게/집/카페, and 손님. English pitfall: don't assume it only labels the person — unlike English 'regular (customer)', 단골 alone can point to the establishment, so 단골 가게 is natural and 'this place is my 단골' makes sense.

usage: to look at the price tag
examples: 가격표 좀 봐 주세요.
Please check the price tag for me.
봐 주세요 asks someone to look on your behalf
이 옷은 가격표가 안 붙어 있어요.
These clothes don't have a price tag on them.
안 붙어 있다 = is not attached (state)
깎지 않고 가격표대로 계산했어요.
I paid the marked price without haggling.
-지 않고 = without doing; 대로 = exactly as
nuance: 가격표 is Sino-Korean 價格表, literally 'price (價格) + table/chart (表)', so it is the physical tag or printed list that displays what something costs. The key is the 표 (表) ending: 가격 alone is the abstract price, while 가격표 is the label you can point to. Its relatives include 정가 (定價, the fixed list price printed on the item) and 영수증 (receipt); the dividing line is timing — you read the 가격표 before buying to learn the set price, but you get an 영수증 after paying as proof. In Korea most stores have firm prices on the 가격표, so haggling is mainly a 시장 (traditional market) thing. It collocates with 보다, 붙이다 (attach), and 대로 (as marked). English pitfall: don't drop the 표 — 가격 is the price concept, but the tag itself must be 가격표, and it is one solid word.

Saying 가격표를 있어요 — possession/existence uses 가, so 가격표가 있어요/없어요.

english: lump-sum payment (paying in full at once)
usage: the one-word reply to the cashier
examples: 일시불로 해 주세요.
Please charge it all at once.
해 주세요 asks the cashier to process it that way
일시불이요.
In full, please.
the standard short answer when asked at checkout
금액이 크지 않으니까 일시불로 결제할게요.
The amount isn't big, so I'll pay it in one go.
-(으)니까 gives the reason; -ㄹ게요 = I'll (intend to)
nuance: 일시불 is Sino-Korean 一時拂, literally 'one (一) + time (時) + pay (拂)', i.e. settling the entire amount in a single charge. Its direct antonym is 할부 (割賦, paying in installments), and these two are the only answers to the question every Korean cashier asks when you hand over a card: 일시불로 하시겠어요? — you reply 일시불이요 or 할부요. A close cousin verb is 결제하다 (to make payment, the formal checkout word) versus casual 계산하다 (to settle up). The dividing line with 할부 is timing of money: 일시불 = whole sum now, 할부 = spread over months. It collocates with 하다, 결제하다, and (으)로. English pitfall: 일시불 is a noun, so you must attach (으)로 to use it adverbially — say 일시불로 해 주세요, never 일시불 해 주세요. Also don't mishear it as a verb; the verb is 결제하다/하다, and 일시불 is the manner.

Its direct antonym is 할부 (割賦, paying in installments); the dividing line is timing of money: 일시불 = whole sum now, 할부 = spread over months. A close cousin verb is 결제하다 (to make payment, the formal checkout word) versus casual 계산하다 (to settle up).
일시불 is Sino-Korean 一時拂, literally 'one (一) + time (時) + pay (拂)'.
일시불 is a noun, so you must attach (으)로 to use it adverbially — say 일시불로 해 주세요, never 일시불 해 주세요. Also don't mishear it as a verb; the verb is 결제하다/하다, and 일시불 is the manner.

mistakes: Confusing 일시불 (pay in full) with its opposite 할부 (pay in installments).
Omitting (으)로 — the noun needs it to act as 'in a lump sum': 일시불로 해 주세요, not 일시불 해 주세요.
Answering 일시불 해요 to the cashier — the natural reply is just 일시불이요 or 일시불로 할게요.

examples: 할부로 해 주세요.
Please put it on installments.
해 주세요 = please process it (for me)
비싸서 3개월 할부로 할게요.
It's pricey, so I'll split it over 3 months.
-아서/어서 = because; 개월 counts months
이거 무이자 할부 되나요?
Is interest-free installment available for this?
되나요? politely asks whether something is possible
nuance: 할부 is Sino-Korean 割賦, literally 'divide (割) + allot/levy (賦)', i.e. splitting a price into several monthly payments — the natural opposite of 일시불 (一時拂, lump sum). At checkout the cashier may follow up with 몇 개월로 해 드릴까요? ('over how many months?'), and big-ticket cards heavily advertise 무이자 할부 (無利子, interest-free installments). Beware the look-alike trap: 할부 (installment) sits right next to 할인 (割引, discount) — same 할 (割, 'cut/divide') root but very different results, one spreads payment, the other lowers price. The dividing line with 일시불 is simply now-vs-later. It collocates with 하다, 결제하다, 개월, and 무이자. English pitfall: like 일시불, 할부 is a noun, so attach (으)로 — 할부로 하다, never 할부 하다. And don't blend it with 할인; saying 할인으로 해 주세요 when you mean installments asks for a price cut instead.

usage: 비용 takes the verb 들다, not 있다
많이 들다 = to take a lot (of cost)
examples: 수리하는 데 비용이 많이 들어요.
Repairing it costs a lot.
-는 데 = for the purpose of doing; the classic 비용 frame
배송 비용은 따로 내야 해요?
Do I have to pay the shipping cost separately?
따로 = separately; -아야 하다 = have to
이사 비용을 줄이려고 직접 옮겼어요.
To cut moving costs, I carried things myself.
-(으)려고 = in order to; 옮기다 = to move things
nuance: 비용 is Sino-Korean 費用, literally 'expend (費) + use (用)', so it is the money (or resources) an activity consumes — shipping, repairs, travel, a wedding. This is exactly where it splits from 값/가격: those name the price of a concrete object, whereas 비용 is the cost of doing something. Its near-synonym is 경비 (經費, 'operating expenses/running costs'), which leans toward organizational or budgeted spending, while 비용 is the everyday word for what a task will run you. The signature grammar is the verb 들다: cost 'goes in', so 비용이 들다 / 비용이 많이 들다. It collocates with 들다, 줄이다 (reduce), 아끼다 (save), and modifiers like 배송/이사/수리. English pitfall: never describe 비용 with 비싸다 — an object can be 비싸다, but a cost 'is a lot' via 비용이 많이 들어요, not 비용이 비싸요. And use 비용, not 값, for the price of an action.

examples: 이거 공짜예요?
Is this one free?
이거 = this thing (casual)
사은품으로 하나 공짜로 줬어요.
They threw one in for free as a giveaway.
사은품 = promotional free gift; 공짜로 = at no cost
세상에 공짜는 없어요.
There's no such thing as a free lunch.
a common saying — 공짜는 없다 = nothing is free
nuance: 공짜 is the warm, colloquial word for something that costs nothing — a freebie you'd grin about. Its near-synonym is the Sino-Korean 무료 (無料, 'no fee'), and the dividing line is register: 무료 is the neutral-to-formal term you read on signs, ads, and apps (무료 배송 'free shipping', 입장 무료 'free admission'), whereas 공짜 is chatty and personal, sometimes even tinged with 'got it for nothing' delight or the cheeky idea of freeloading (공짜 좋아하다 'to love free stuff'). Treat 공짜 as native/colloquial in feel; don't force a hanja onto it. It collocates with 주다 (give), 받다 (get), and noun-modifying use (공짜 커피). English pitfall: it's a noun, so for 'for free' attach (으)로 — 공짜로 받았어요, never 공짜 받았어요. And in formal or written contexts switch to 무료; writing 공짜 입장 on an official notice sounds too casual.

usage: to do a deal / do business
거래 + 를 하다; verb form is 거래하다
직접 (直接) = directly, face to face
examples: 현금 거래도 돼요?
Can we do it as a cash deal too?
-도 돼요? = is ... also okay?
당근마켓에서 직접 거래로 샀어요.
I bought it via in-person deal on Danggeun Market.
직접 거래 = meeting up to trade, common secondhand
은행과 오래 거래해 왔어요.
I've banked with them for a long time.
거래하다 also = to have ongoing business dealings
nuance: 거래 is Sino-Korean 去來, literally 'go (去) + come (來)' — the back-and-forth of money and goods, hence a transaction or deal. Its near-synonym is 매매 (賣買, 'sell-buy'), and the dividing line is scope: 매매 specifically denotes buying-and-selling (often property or stocks: 부동산 매매), while 거래 is broader, covering any dealing — a shop sale, a bank relationship (은행과 거래하다), or a person-to-person 중고 거래 (secondhand trade). In the huge secondhand market, 직접 거래 means meeting in person to hand over cash and item. It collocates with 하다, 현금/직접/안전, and 끝나다/성사되다 (be concluded). The verb is 거래하다, which can mean both 'make a one-off deal' and 'have ongoing business with'. English pitfall: don't confuse 거래 (a deal/dealing) with 거래처 (去來處, a regular business client/account) — the added 처 (處, 'place') makes it the counterparty firm, not the transaction itself.
